newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Eurotunnel rules out systems failure in fire.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Eurotunnel rules out systems failure in fire.

text.p: Anglo-French Channel Tunnel operator Eurotunnel Plc on Thursday admitted delays in dealing with a fire last year but said the blaze was not due to mechanical or systems failure.
The company's internal inquiry reported "avoidable delays" in emergency procedures in tackling the fire, which injured 34 people, and said it would implement measures to improve safety.

French judicial authorities are still investigating the exact cause of the fire, which broke out on a truck-carrying shuttle train and severely hit Eurotunnel's passenger and freight services between Britain and France.
No lives were lost in the blaze.
The company's statement did not mention the design of its open-sided freight wagons, which had been criticised by British firefighters for allegedly helping to intensify the the blaze.

"We have, of course, learned lessons from this incident and have already implemented a number of important changes in procedures, equipment, manning levels and training," chairmen Patrick Ponsolle and Robert Malpas said in a statement.
The company is due to hold a news conference on the report later on Thursday in Calais.
Eurotunnel said it expected to re-open heavy goods vehicles (HGV) shuttle services before the middle of June and complete repairs on the south tunnel by mid-May.
The statement gave no estimate of the fire's financial impact on the debt-laden company.
In January, Eurotunnel said it had a substantial loss of revenue in the last seven weeks of 1996 due to the disruption in service caused by the November 18 blaze.
Eurotunnel's shares were little changed after its report, firming 0.5 pence to 71 pence in London and staying at about 6.40 francs in Paris.
The company's inquiry attributed delays in emergency measures to the complexity of some procedures and to human and technical problems in communication.

Eurotunnel said procedural changes would include more systematic checks on trucks at the time of loading, better surveillance of departing shuttles and more direct contact with the railway control centre.
It also planned to install additional fire suppression systems in the rail tunnels by 1999.

"The Channel Tunnel was designed to be one of the safest transport systems in the world. The changes we have announced today will make the system even safer and give us the confidence to re-open our HGV shuttle services," the chairmen said.
Separately, Eurotunnel said traffic carried in March by the Le Shuttle tourist service dipped to 153,796 vehicles, including coaches, from some 158,494 a year earlier.

"These figures are close to those for March 1996, so are very satisfactory, particularly taking into account the fact that our capacity has been reduced by half due to the repair works currently being carried out in the tunnel," the company said.
While Le Shuttle results fell, traffic on the high-speed Eurostar passenger train service shot up to 500,899 passengers in March from 389,069 in the year-ago period.
The amount of rail freight transported also rose, increasing to 230,753 tonnes from 207,417 in March 1996.
